1:
The word spirit here means a man, and they say so almost with one voice. Gill takes it either of a doctrine claiming to come from the Spirit or of a teacher professing to be sent by him; Calvin fixes on the teacher and rewrites the whole passage in those terms, so that the mark distinguishes the teacher of God from the teacher of antichrist; Clarke explains the usage historically, since in those early days every teacher professed inspiration because the prophets had all come so accredited; Wesley glosses it in three words, whereby any teacher is actuated. Robertson catches the force of the tense, that the command is to stop believing, some having already been carried off by the errors then rampant, and he adds that credulity is gullibility and that believers still fall easy victims to the latest fads in spiritualistic humbuggery. What the trying amounts to he takes from metallurgy: put them to the acid test as the assayer does his metals, and the coin that stands is approved while the other is rejected. Clarke and Wesley both name the touchstone rather than the method, the word of revelation already given, to the law and to the testimony.

Two of them draw pastoral conclusions from the existence of counterfeits, and they run opposite ways. Henry argues from the counterfeit back to the genuine: imitation presupposes something worth imitating, so the very existence of false claims proves that real communications had been made, and God will take the way of his own wisdom even where it lies open to abuse — which is why a judgment of discretion is left with the disciples rather than a rule of blanket trust. Calvin looks at the same fact and sees the danger in the other direction. Satan works perpetually to pollute the purity of the gospel with a variety of errors, and his own age had produced sects so monstrous that many, not knowing where to turn, threw over all care for religion; and he calls that the most foolish course of all, since by shunning the light of truth they cast themselves into the dark. Barnes, more coolly, lays out how the chapter will proceed and what evidence will count, that the Spirit is known by the confession made, by what is denied, by not having the spirit of this world, and by hearing those whom God has sent.

On the confession itself two cautions are entered. Barnes denies that a form of words settles anything, since the point is not that saying it proves a man a Christian but that holding and teaching it marks him an advocate of truth rather than an apostle of error; and he rejects the proposed rendering that would make the clause say Jesus who came in the flesh is the Christ. Robertson secures it grammatically, preferring the participle to the infinitive, so that the phrase describes Jesus as already come in actual humanity and not in the phantom body the Docetists allowed him. Calvin takes the two halves apart: that Christ came proves he was already with the Father and so eternal, and that he came in flesh means he took our own nature and became our brother, sin excepted. Then the text divides them. Barnes reports the Latin reading that has the false teacher dissolving or dividing Jesus, traces it through the Fathers, and rejects it as having no real authority and being manifestly of Latin origin, probably a marginal note that worked its way in. Robertson keeps it in view as an allusion to a second heresy, one splitting Jesus from Christ where the earlier clause met the Docetists; and he and Clarke agree that the repeated words about the flesh in this verse are no part of the text.
4:
The victory is spoken of as done, and each of them accounts for the tense differently. Robertson takes it as the calm confidence of a finished thing. Calvin explains why: eagerness slackens when the issue of a fight is in doubt, so they are told they have conquered although still in the middle of the contest, and he widens the promise to every struggle with the world and the flesh, since we fight with weapons not our own and so become conquerors by the very fighting. Barnes presses the same point negatively, that no part of the victory was their own strength, and draws from it that a Christian in conflict with sin or error should never despair. Henry finds a strong preserver within them and calls it a great happiness to be under that influence; Gill grounds it in election, so that they could not be finally and totally seduced; Clarke makes the overcoming a matter of testimony, theirs proceeding from one Spirit having invalidated the testimony that proceeded from another. Calvin also settles who is meant by them, referring it back to the false prophets and noting that this writer commonly picks up an antecedent at some distance.

Augustine takes the passage somewhere none of the others go, making the present world the desert and the faithful the people crossing it. They wandered, but with God to guide could not wander astray, and their forty years were made up of very few stations, so they were held back because they were being trained and not because they were abandoned. Then the application: if you would not die of thirst in this wilderness, drink charity, which is the fountain God has been pleased to set here so that we do not faint on the road, and which we shall drink more abundantly when we reach our own country. He binds it to the prayer they had just heard read, since we have covenanted with God that we should forgive as we would be forgiven, and forgiveness is nothing but charity at work — take charity from the heart and hatred takes the room, and hatred does not know how to forgive. Gill describes the other party plainly, men still under the dominion of sin who take gain for godliness and admire persons for the advantage in it; Robertson puts it in one line, that the false prophets and the world are in perfect unison, and Wesley notes that the world hears them with approbation.

Calvin refuses the English rendering of the next clause, since the preposition never means concerning, and argues from a use elsewhere that it means according to, so the sense is that they speak by the world's own principles. He also notices what the argument rests on: the claim to be of God is the easiest of boasts, and the false prophets make it as loudly, deceiving under the mask of God, so the believer must be content with the fewness of the faithful and remember that wide rejection is no reflection on the gospel's authority. Barnes observes that the writer can simply assume his own standing and reason from it, and turns that into a question — why should not every Christian and every minister live so that no one would think to dispute their integrity? Clarke supplies a rough test in the other direction, that the teaching prized by the gay and garish multitude lays on no restraint, prescribes no cross-bearing, and leaves a man his favourite sins; Barnes offers the same test turned inward, that a man may learn much about himself by asking what sort of people are pleased with him. Robertson accepts the test and then qualifies it, granting that he has felt the cold stare of the worldling, but warning that rejection may also be owing to our not speaking the truth in love.
7:
Henry piles up the titles: God is the fountain, author, parent and commander of love, so the new nature in his children is the offspring of it and love comes down from heaven. Barnes reduces the same claim to three propositions, that all true love originates in God, that real love proves we have his Spirit, and that it makes us more like him — then fences it, since the verse plainly does not mean that a man who loves his wife and children, or his partner in business, or his farms, is thereby born of God. Robertson allows the widest form of the claim, that even human love is a reflection of something in the divine nature itself. Calvin narrows it from the other side, refusing to count the love that merely returns what friends have given, and holding that the true knowledge of God necessarily produces love in whoever has it. Clarke turns the proposition into a measure — he that loves most has most of God in him — and Gill supplies the reason the exhortation returns here at all, that where worldly men cleave to false teachers those on the side of truth should hold together.

On the three words that follow they divide sharply. Wesley says the little sentence brought the writer more sweetness while he wrote it than the whole world can bring, and observes that God is styled holy and righteous and wise but never holiness or righteousness in the abstract as he is here said to be love — which makes this his reigning attribute, shedding a glory over all the rest. Clarke makes the identical observation and goes further, calling love the essence of the divine nature and the other attributes only modifications of it, and then turns the verse into a weapon: God has made no one for perdition nor rendered it impossible by any necessitating decree for a fallen soul to find mercy, so how can a decree of absolute unconditional reprobation stand in the presence of such a text? Calvin denies the premise both are working from. He knows the refinements, and complains that the ancients perverted the passage to prove the divinity of the Spirit; the sentence does not speak of God's essence at all, only of what he is found to be by us, as calling him light described not his substance but his shining. Robertson polices the grammar between them, noting the predicate has no article, so the writer says God is love and not that love is God, the two being far from interchangeable.

Calvin grants many other proofs of that love — creation, the dominion given us, our preservation, our light and understanding, none admitting any explanation but gratuitous kindness — yet calls this the principal evidence, so that whenever we look at the Son the truth is confirmed to us. Barnes measures it in five quantities: the worth of the soul, its exposure to death, the greatness of the gift, the greatness of the sorrows, and the blessedness we are raised to; and adds that whether saved or lost we shall have an ever-expanding view of it. Gill will not let the love be general, restricting it to the elect and pushing it behind the sending, to the choice in Christ, the appointment of a Saviour and the covenant made on their account. Robertson keeps to the words, insisting the phrase means in us and not among us or to us, and marking the change of tense between the permanent mission here and the single act following. On that verse Calvin turns polemical in his turn, since if a man were chosen because God foresaw him worthy of love, this doctrine that God loved first would not stand; and Barnes distinguishes the two loves, not complacency in our character but benevolence toward our welfare.
11:
The inference from God's love to ours is sharpened by three of them. Barnes gives it as a set of reasons and then reverses the direction: there are far stronger reasons why we should love each other than there ever were why God should love us. Clarke draws the corollary, that since we were loved without desert we must not suspend our love on a neighbour's moral worth or his love to us, and that a love with God for motive and model will never fail. Calvin puts the same negatively, that our love must not be mercenary, since to consult our own advantage or to repay the good offices of friends is self-love and not love of others. Augustine begins his homily with the difficulty of keeping so large a command: love is a sweet word but sweeter the deed, and though business draws us different ways so that the tongue cannot always speak of it, the thing itself may always be kept. He illustrates from the Alleluia then being sung, which fills only a few moments of an hour, whereas the man who praises God by his life is doing it always, since works of mercy, chastity and sobriety are practised in public or at home, speaking or silent, occupied or idle, being all of them within.

Cyril takes the invisibility literally and presses it. The incorporeal cannot be subject to bodily sight, and the prophet said to have seen saw only the likeness of the glory and fell to the earth from fear at that; anyone attempting to behold God himself would lose his life, which is why God in great loving-kindness spread the heaven as a veil over his Godhead, that we should not perish. Gill turns the same fact into an argument for the brethren: God cannot be seen and conversed with as one friend converses with another, so love is not increased by sight and company, and the visible saints are given us to love instead. Barnes states the rule — we cannot become acquainted with him by sight, but we may by love — and Clarke shortens it, that we may feel him though we cannot see him. Calvin notes the same words in the Gospel with a narrower point, that God is not otherwise known than as revealed in Christ, whereas here the truth is extended, the power of God being grasped by faith and love. On the perfecting Barnes cautions that neither we nor our love are perfect, only that loving others carries out our love towards him.

The Spirit given is the second proof. Robertson marks the perfect tense of the giving and calls the gift itself the evidence of fellowship; Barnes points to what it produces, the love and joy and peace of the familiar list; Calvin closes the circle, since love is the fruit of the Spirit and cannot be exercised unless the Spirit puts forth his power, so whoever boasts of having God while not loving the brethren is convicted by that want. Then the apostolic testimony, where they part over what seeing means. Gill lists what the eyes took in, the miracles, the dying and rising and going up; Henry sets out the article in five heads, the Son's relation to the Father, his office as Saviour of the world, the mission that grounds it, the seeing that assures it and the witness that follows. Calvin denies that any sort of seeing is meant: it is the seeing that belongs to faith, by which they recognised the glory of God in Christ, and it flows from the illumination of the Spirit. Robertson adds that the title Saviour of the world stands nowhere else in these writings but on Samaritan lips, and Wesley makes the two things named here, the communion of the Spirit and the confession of the Son, the criteria of abiding.
15:
All of them guard the confession against becoming a form of words. Gill produces two hard cases, the devils who owned the title and the centurion at the cross who knew nothing of communion with God; Barnes says flatly that saying it insincerely proves nothing; Robertson holds that the confession implies surrender and obedience and not lip service; Wesley adds the condition that makes it cost something, an open confession in the face of opposition and danger; and Clarke explains why so much weight falls on this article, the false teachers having denied the reality of the incarnation. Calvin turns the next verse into a definition, that to know and believe is to know by believing, so that an uncertain or doubtful opinion is a different thing altogether from faith; and he lays out the chain in order, that faith brings God to dwell in us, that God is love, and that therefore love must be found wherever he abides. Barnes puts the same sentence to another use, asking what trial cannot be borne by a man who can say from the depths of himself that God is love.

Whose love is made perfect divides them four ways. Gill weighs the versions reading it of God's love with us and decides against them, since God's love admits no degrees and cannot be made more perfect by ours; Calvin reads it of God's love notwithstanding, as poured out so abundantly that it appears complete; Barnes takes it of the love within us; and Robertson construes the phrase with the verb instead, so that it marks cooperation and means that God works with man. On the boldness they agree and describe it differently. Calvin states the natural case first: we dread God's presence justly, since he is Judge and our guilt brings death and hell to mind whenever we think of him, which is why men shun him as far as they can. Henry pictures the reversal, of those who can lift their heads and look the Judge in the face knowing him for friend and advocate. Augustine, opening his last homily on the epistle, finds charity already doing that work in smaller matters, since where it is absent the man who exacts his due is bitter, and where it is present both the exacting and the paying are sweet and the labour becomes almost no labour at all.

Then the fear. Robertson makes it the dread of a bondman rather than the reverence of a son, notes that the word for its torment carries discipline and not merely penalty, and quotes Bengel's four conditions of men: without fear or love, with fear and no love, with both, and with love and no fear. Wesley gives that ladder in his own words as the natural man, the awakened, the babe and the father in Christ. Gill sorts the fear the same way, excluding the filial fear that is the beginning of wisdom and referring the verse either to the fear of men or to the dread of the judgment. Calvin refuses the whole distinction. He knows the passage is commonly explained by setting servile fear against voluntary reverence, and grants the doctrine true, but says it has nothing in common with this text, since what the writer teaches is that the love of God known by faith gives a calm beyond the reach of fear; and he adds that he regards what the apostle means, not what others think. Clarke describes the man still short of it, who has many heavenly drawings and sits with Christ some moments on a throne of love, yet dreads the day of judgment because of the evils he finds in his heart. Cyril applies the verse where the angel divides the women from the soldiers, telling these to fear and those not.
19:
The first clause can be read as a statement or a summons, the Greek form being the same either way. Robertson takes it as a statement and notes that no object is expressed. Calvin allows both and prefers the statement, remarking that the sense would come out much the same on either reading. Clarke reports that two of the old versions turn it into a summons, let us therefore love him because he first loved us. Barnes raises the deeper question. If being loved first is not merely how we came to love but the whole ground of loving, the love is mere selfishness; so he distinguishes, granting that benefits received are a proper reason while insisting that the original ground is the excellence of the divine character itself, which a holy being would love apart from any benefit and without a thought of his own destiny. Against that Clarke lists three grounds without ranking them, that we find he has loved us, that obligation and gratitude follow, and that his love shed abroad in the heart is the seed our love grows from; and Gill pushes the priority back as far as it will go, into election and the covenant, so that grace brings love with it rather than finding it.

The argument from the seen to the unseen is stated by Barnes as an appeal to human nature as it stands, since we are likelier to love someone familiar than a stranger. Calvin, alone among them, admits the argument looks weak and says why. It reasons from the lesser to the greater, and two things spoil the comparison: the love God has to us comes by faith and not by sight at all, and the two loves are unlike, since God draws us by infinite goodness while men are often worthy of hatred. His answer is that the writer assumes what should be plain, that God presents himself in those who bear his image and requires of us toward them the services he does not need himself; and he adds that a shared nature, mutual need and daily dealing ought to draw us together unless we are harder than iron. Gill puts the contradiction bluntly, that profession and hatred agree no better than black with white or hot with cold, while Barnes takes the edge off the charge of lying by noting that no deliberate deceit need be meant, only that the profession is false.

Clarke gives the passage a target. Much of the epistle seems to him aimed at those who professed great love to God while hating the nations outside, a leaven some carried into the church; and he recalls that it took a vision to free even Peter from it. He also distinguishes the two springs of love toward a brother, his excellences, which draw a love of delight, and his miseries, which draw a love of pity. On the closing command Barnes presses the obligation, that the second binds exactly as the first does, so a man who feels the one and not the other has no evidence of anything; Calvin calls it the strongest argument in the chapter because it rests on the authority of Christ, and states the rule that we must so begin with God that a passage is made at the same time to men. Wesley draws the sharpest conclusion of the six. The brother is to be loved whatever his opinions or his manner of worship, purely because he bears the image of God; bigotry is precisely the want of that pure and universal love, since a bigot loves only those who hold his opinions and keep his way of worship, and loves them for that and not for Christ's sake.
